extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical literature, translators, and readers studying Horace's Satires
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging literary satire (as exemplified by Horace), including moral aims, stylistic features (meter, concision), audience/venue considerations, and standards distinguishing satire from higher poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between true poet and conversational verse
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who composes verses that are 'really more like conversation' should not be called a true poet; the true poet has imaginative power and lofty utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: presence of 'imaginative power' and 'lofty utterance' beyond mere metrical beat. Example: comedy (and Horace's conversational lines) may lack the fire and force of inspiration; if you remove the metrical element and change word order you get plain prose. Implication: label 'poet' reserved for writers with transcendent diction and thought, not merely for anyone who writes metrical talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical element as necessary distinguishing feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse that differs from prose chiefly by a 'regular beat' (pede certo) is nearer to prose than to high poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: preserve metrical integrity and the musical/rhythmic qualities that distinguish verse from prose. Beware that mere rhythm without imaginative force may not suffice to merit the name 'poem'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should be social/general rather than personal malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace maintains his satire is 'not personal, but rather social and general in its application' and 'does not indulge in the invective of Old Comedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write merely to attack individuals; aim satire at broader social follies and customs. Avoid wholesale personal invective and scandal-mongering; follow the 'New' rather than the Old comedic spirit when seeking moral or social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid malicious informing and spiteful intent
rubrics_metrics.description: The author denies being an informer or writing to give pain, and rejects 'spiteful' or 'venom' unadulterate in his pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral constraint: the satirist should not aim to wound or ruin private individuals. If criticism is sharp, it should be justified, tempered, and aimed at correction or public good rather than private malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples of vices to deter vice (didactic aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet was trained by his father 'to steer clear of follies' by 'branding them, one by one, by his examples' — i.e., noting vices as warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire has an educative function: exposing faults so readers may avoid them. Prefer illustrative anecdotes/exempla that instruct rather than merely scandalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality in criticism and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Let there be 'a rule to assign just penalties to offences, lest you flay with the terrible scourge what calls for the strap' — do not treat all crimes equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satirically judging wrongdoing, distinguish degrees of offense; avoid moralizing that flattens distinctions between minor and serious faults. Tone and severity should match the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbosity and carelessness — prefer quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucilius's chief fault is described as being 'careless and verbose, more interested in the quantity than in the quality of his work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not emulate hurried, abundant production (e.g., dictating 'two hundred lines' in an hour). Edit ruthlessly: remove muddy or unpleasant passages; value careful composition over sheer output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lazy or sloppy craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucilius 'was wordy, and too lazy to put up with the trouble of writing correctly' — a textual fault to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to craft: correct diction, ordering of words, and metrical polish. Laziness that results in muddled verse harms the satirist's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invent or falsify — honesty about facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticized behaviors include 'fingere qui non visa potest' (one who invents what he has not seen) and the inability 'commissa tacere qui nequit' (who cannot keep entrusted secrets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inventing episodes or attributing false acts to real people. If using real incidents, be factual and cautious about exposing confidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from backbiting and failing to defend friends
rubrics_metrics.description: The satirist should not be 'absentem qui rodit amicura' (one who bites an absent friend) or 'qui non defendit alio culpante' (who does not defend someone when another finds fault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical standard: loyalty and fairness; avoid punching down via anonymous or cowardly attacks. Satire should not be a covering for betrayal of personal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and venue sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace insists he recites only to friends 'idque coactus, non ubivis coramve quibuslibet' and criticizes those who recite in the Forum or baths where 'suave locus voci resonat' but taste may be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate audiences and settings: avoid public exhibitionism that seeks cheap applause. Consider whether time, place, and listeners make a reading tasteful or in bad season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate liberty of speech with paternal/moral constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet asks listeners to grant indulgence for jocose speech ('si forte iocosius'), explaining this liberty was taught by his father who used exempla to deter vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise freedom of expression, but within a framework of moral restraint and self-scrutiny; request indulgence when humor risks offense and be prepared to justify it as corrective rather than malicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid courting popularity by besmirching others for laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproof of those who 'captat risus hominum famamque dicacis' (seek the laughter and reputation of a wit) and who will 'spare not a single friend' to get a laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize social status or a laughing reputation over integrity; satire that aims primarily for applause at others' expense is censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune out 'muddy' or offensive material
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucilius's 'muddy stream' contained material 'you would like to remove' — a call to excise unpleasant parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit to remove gross or unnecessary nastiness; retain forceful critique but eliminate gratuitous coarseness or passages that detract from overall artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that some styles repel readers — accept limits of audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace notes 'this style is abhorrent to some' and that 'all of these dread verses and detest the poet' — certain manners of satire will offend many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that satirical tone or subject may alienate parts of the readership; decide whether to write for broad popularity or restricted, sympathetic audiences, and accept consequences.
